'''''Leucaena leucocephala''''' is a small fast-growing [[Mimosoideae|mimosoid]] tree native to southern Mexico and northern [[Central America]] (Belize and Guatemala).<ref name="GRIN"/><ref name = Hughes>{{cite book | last = Hughes | first = Colin E. | title = Monograph of Leucaena (Leguminosae-Mimosoideae) | series = Systematic botany monographs v. 55 | year = 1998 | isbn = 978-0-912861-55-5 }}</ref> It is now naturalized throughout the tropics including parts of Asia.

Common names include '''white leadtree''',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=LELE10 |title=PLANTS Profile for ''Leucaena leucocephala'' (white leadtree) |work=PLANTS Database |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=2009-09-19}}</ref> '''white popinac''',<ref  name="GRIN"/> '''horse tamarind''',<ref name="GRIN"/> '''ipil-ipil''',<ref name="FTL">{{cite book |editor-last1=Shelton |editor-first1=H.M. |editor-last2=Brewbaker |editor-first2=J.L. |chapter=2.1 Leucaena leucocephala – the Most Widely Used Forage Tree Legume |chapter-url=http://www.fao.org/ag/agp/agpc/doc/publicat/gutt-shel/x5556e06.htm |title=Forage tree legumes in tropical agriculture  |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations]] |access-date=24 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171108181232/http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/AGPC/doc/Publicat/Gutt-shel/x5556e06.htm |archive-date=8 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Matthews |first1=Donald Maxwell|series=Forestry Bureau Bulletin|volume=13 |title=Ipil-ipil: A firewood and reforestation crop (Leucaena glauca (L.) Benth) |date=1914 |publisher=Bureau of Printing, Philippine Islands, Bureau of Forestry |location=Manila}}</ref> '''koa haole''',<ref name=Leucaena>{{cite web |title=Koa haole, leucaena |url=https://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/gsp/doc/Forestry/Little_Skolmen_CFT/CFT_Leucaena_leucocephala.pdf |work=Common Forest Trees of Hawaii (Native and Introduced) |access-date=3 October 2024}}</ref> '''tan-tan,'''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants – Buck Island Reef |url=https://www.nps.gov/buis/learn/nature/plants.htm |publisher=[[National Park Service]] (US) |access-date=19 January 2023}}</ref> and '''tangantangan'''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Craig |first=Robert J. |date=1993 |title=Regeneration of Native Mariana Island Forest in Disturbed Habitats |url=https://micronesica.org/sites/default/files/262_article_01ed.pdf |journal=Micronesica |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=99-108 |via=Micronesica}}</ref>

''Leucaena leucocephala'' is used for a variety of purposes, such as fencing, [[soil fertility]], [[firewood]], [[Fiber crop|fiber]], and [[livestock]] [[fodder]].

== Description ==
[[File:Folhas de leucena (Leucaena leucocephala) em Bagé, RS, Brasil.jpg|thumb|Leaves]]

''Leucaena leucocephala'' is a small tree, growing up to {{Convert|7-18|m}}. Its bark is grey and cracked. The branches have no thorns, each branch has 6–8 pairs of leaf stalks that bear 11–23 pairs of leaflets, each leaflet is 8–17 mm<!-- max length fr Corner --> long with a pale green surface and whitish underneath.<ref name="FTL"/><ref name="Corner"/>

Its inflorescence is a cream-coloured puff with many stamens. They produce flat and straight seed pods measuring {{Convert abbreviated|13-18|cm}} long that matures from a green colour to a brown; one pod contains between 15 and 30 seeds.<ref name="FTL"/>

==Ecology==
''Leucaena leucocephala'' is susceptible to insect infestations. In the 1980s, a widespread loss in [[Southeast Asia]] was due to pest attack by [[Jumping plant louse|psyllids]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carter |first=Jane |date=June 1995 |title=Alley farming: have resource-poor farmers benefited? |url=https://media.odi.org/documents/2985.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240616052020/https://media.odi.org/documents/2985.pdf |archive-date=2024-06-16 |website=ODI}}</ref>

In India, this tree was initially promoted for afforestation due to its fast-growing nature. However, it is now considered unsuitable for urban planting because of its tendency to get uprooted in rain and wind. Eight of every ten trees uprooted by wind in [[Pune]] are ''L. leucocephala''.<ref>{{cite news |last=Das |first=Dipannita |date=8 May 2011 |title=Activists want Pune Municipal Corporation to allow cutting of subabul trees in city |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/pune/Activists-want-Pune-Municipal-Corporation-to-allow-cutting-of-subabul-trees-in-city/articleshow/8200176.cms |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120715011056/http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/pune/Activists-want-Pune-Municipal-Corporation-to-allow-cutting-of-subabul-trees-in-city/articleshow/8200176.cms |archive-date=15 July 2012 |access-date=9 May 2011 |newspaper=[[The Times of India]]}}</ref>

==Invasive properties==
''Leucaena leucocephala'' is considered one of the 100 worst invasive species by the Invasive Species Specialist Group of the [[IUCN Species Survival Commission]].<ref name="GISB">{{cite web |title=Leucaena leucocephala (tree) |url=http://www.invasivespecies.net/database/species/ecology.asp?si=23&fr=1&sts=sss&lang=EN |access-date=2010-01-18 |work=Global Invasive Species Database |publisher=Invasive Species Specialist Group}}</ref>

It is a highly [[invasive species]] in the arid parts of [[Taiwan]], [[The Bahamas]], the [[Hawaiian Islands]], [[Fiji]], [[Puerto Rico]], [[Hong Kong]], [[South Africa]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.invasives.org.za/legislation/item/270-leucaena-leucaena-leucocephala|title=Leucaena | Leucaena leucocephala|access-date=2017-10-04|archive-date=2017-10-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171005050614/http://www.invasives.org.za/legislation/item/270-leucaena-leucaena-leucocephala|url-status=dead|website=Invasive Species South Africa}}</ref> and northern [[Australia]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=T20 |title=Leucaena ''Leucaena leucocephala'' |work=Weed Identification & Information |publisher=Australian Weeds Strategy |access-date=2009-09-19 |archive-date=2009-09-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090930022449/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=T20 |url-status=dead }}</ref> as well as in northern [[Malay Peninsula]],<ref name="Corner" /> [[South America]] and [[Southern Europe]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fonseca |first1=N.G. |last2=Jacobi |first2=C.M. |date=2011 |title=Desempenho germinativo da invasora ''Leucaena leucocephala'' (Lam.) de Wit. e comparação com ''Caesalpinia ferrea'' Mart. ex Tul. e ''Caesalpinia pulcherrima'' (L.) Sw. (Fabaceae) |language=pt |journal=Acta Botanica Brasilica |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=191–197 |doi=10.1590/S0102-33062011000100022 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The plant is also found in parts of the U.S., including [[California]], [[Arizona]], [[Texas]], [[Hawaii]], and [[Florida]].<ref name="usda">{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=LELE10|title=Leucaena leucocephala (Lam.) de Wit white leadtree|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture|access-date=8 June 2010}}</ref>
[[File:Leucaena leucocephala Wood in Hong Kong.jpg|thumb|240px|''Leucaena leucocephala'' wood and bark]]

It grows quickly and forms dense thickets that crowd out all native vegetation.<ref>Kuo, Yau-Lun. "Ecological Characteristics of Three Invasive Plants (Leucaena Leucocephala, Mikania Micrantha, and Stachytarpheta Urticaefolia) in Southern Taiwan." 12 1 2003.http://www.agnet.org/library/eb/541/ (accessed 3 24 2008).</ref>

In urban areas, it is an especially unwanted species, growing along arid roadsides, in carparks, and on abandoned land.<ref>[http://www.devb.gov.hk/filemanager/technicalcirculars/en/upload/16/1/C-2006-03-0-1.pdf Tree Preservation]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Leucaena leucocephala|url=http://www.hkflora.com/qef/site_peak/plant/show_plant.php?plantnum=11751|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305141547/http://hkflora.com/qef/site_peak/plant/show_plant.php?plantnum=11751|archive-date=2016-03-05|access-date=2017-08-04|website=Hong Kong Flora and Vegetation}}</ref>

== Toxicity ==
The [[seed]]s of ''Leucaena leucocephala'' contain [[mimosine]], an [[amino acid]] known to be [[Toxin|toxic]] to non[[ruminant]] [[vertebrate]]s.<ref name="fao.org">{{Cite web |title=2.1 Leucaena leucocephala – the Most Widely Used Forage Tree Legume |url=http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/AGPC/doc/Publicat/Gutt-shel/x5556e06.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160715130422/http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/AGPC/doc/Publicat/Gutt-shel/x5556e06.htm |archive-date=2016-07-15 |access-date=2017-08-04 |website=www.fao.org}}</ref>

== Uses ==
During the 1970s and 1980s, ''Leucaena leucocephala'' was promoted as a "miracle tree" for its multiple uses.<ref name="fao.org" /> It has also been described as a "conflict tree" because it is used for forage production but spreads like a weed in some places.<ref name="GISB" />

The [[legume]] is promoted in several countries of Southeast Asia (at least [[Burma]], [[Cambodia]], [[Indonesia]], [[Laos]],<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite news |date=2011-06-15 |title=Farmers to grow leucaena for animal feed |newspaper=Vientiane Times}}</ref> and [[Thailand]]), most importantly as a source of quality animal feed, but also for residual use for firewood or [[charcoal]] production.

=== Culinary ===
The young pods are edible and occasionally eaten in [[Pecel|Javanese vegetable salad with spicy peanut sauce]], and [[Buntil|spicy fish wrapped in papaya or taro leaves]] in Indonesia, and in [[Tam mak hoong|papaya salad]] in [[Laos]]<ref name="ReferenceA" /> and Thailand, where they are known as {{Lang|th-Latn|phak krathin}} ({{langx|th|ผักกระถิน}}).<ref>{{usurped|[https://web.archive.org/web/20111008191140/http://www.aseanbiodiversity.info/Abstract/53002579.pdf ASEAN Biodiversity]}}</ref> In Mexico it is eaten in soups and also inside tacos, it is known as ''guaje''.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}} Cooking is thought to remove most of the poison.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2010-06-17 |title=Leucaena leucocephala - White Leadtree, Lead Tree, Koa Haole, Ekoa, Leucaena, Horse Tamarind, Jumbie Bean, White Popinac |url=https://wildlifeofhawaii.com/flowers/1266/leucaena-leucocephala-white-leadtree/ |access-date=2025-07-09 |website=Hawaiian Plants and Tropical Flowers |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Forage and fodder ===
The legume provides an excellent source of high-protein cattle fodder.<ref name="purdue">{{cite web |title=Leucaena leucocephala (Lam.) deWit. |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/leucaena_leucocephala.html |access-date=8 June 2010 |publisher=hort.purdue.edu}}</ref>  However, the fodder contains [[mimosine]], a toxic amino acid. Horses and donkeys which are fed it lose their hair.

In many cases this acid is metabolized by ruminants to goitrogenic DHP [3-hydroxy-4(1H) pyridone] in the [[rumen]],<ref>Hammond, A. C. 1995. Leucaena toxicosis and its control in ruminants. J. Animal Sci. 73: 1487–1492.</ref><ref>Allison, M. J., A.  C. Hammond, and R. J. Jones.  1990.  Detection of ruminal bacteria that degrade toxic dihydroxypyridine compounds produced from mimosine. Appl. Environ. Microbiol. 56: 590–594.</ref> but in some geographical areas, ruminants lack the organisms (such as ''[[Synergistes jonesii]]'') that can degrade DHP.

In such cases, toxicity problems from ingestion of ''Leucaena'' have sometimes been overcome by infusing susceptible animals with rumen fluid from ruminants that possess such organisms,<ref>Allison, M. J., W. R. Mayberry, C. S. Mcsweeney, and D. A. Stahl. 1992.  Synergistes jonesii, gen. nov., sp. nov.: a rumen bacterium that degrades toxic pyridinediols. Syst. Appl. Microbiol. 15: 522–529.</ref> and more recently by [[microbial inoculant|inoculating]] cattle [[rumen|rumina]] with such organisms cultured in vitro.<ref>Graham, S. R., S. A. Dalzell, Nguyen Trong Ngu, C. K. Davis, D. Greenway, C. S. McSweeney, and H. M. Shelton. 2013.  Efficacy, persistence and presence of Synergistes jonesii in cattle grazing leucaena in Queensland: on-farm observations pre-and post-inoculation. Animal Prod. Sci. 53: 1065–1074.</ref><ref name="Qld-inoculum">{{cite web |date=2020-08-26 |title=''Leucaena'' inoculum for cattle |url=http://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/farms-fishing-forestry/agriculture/livestock/cattle/leucaena-inoculum-cattle |access-date=2021-08-12 |website=Business Queensland}}</ref>

Such measures have facilitated ''Leucaena'' use for fodder in Australia and elsewhere.<ref name="Qld-inoculum" />

===Green manure and biomass production===
[[Image:Leucena.jpg|thumb|Tree]]
''Leucaena leucocephala'' has been considered for [[biomass]] production because its reported yield of foliage corresponds to a dried mass of {{formatnum:2000–20000}} kg/ha/year, and that of wood 30–40 m<sup>3</sup>/ha/year, with up to twice those amounts in favorable climates. In India it is being promoted for both fodder and energy.<ref>[https://www.thebetterindia.com/172164/subabul-tree-fodder-fuel-nitrogen-environment-animals/ Subabul Reloaded: How One Tree Could Be the Answer to India’s Fodder, Fuel Needs; Published] in [[The Better India]], 11 February 2019</ref>

It is also efficient in [[nitrogen fixation]], at more than 500 kg/ha/year.

It has a very fast growth rate: young trees reach a height of more than {{Convert abbreviated|20|ft}} in two to three years.

===Pulpwood for paper industry===
The wood of ''Leucaena leucocephala'' is used for making pulp in the [[pulp and paper industry]]. In the southern and central states of India, it is the most important pulpwood species for making pulp. It has huge positive socio-economic impact on the livelihood of the small farmers where ''Leucaena leucocephala'' is grown as an industrial crop. This provides an alternative crop to the farmers of [[Andhra Pradesh]] and [[Telangana]], where they are also growing cotton and chillies.

=== Potential as bioherbicidal agent ===
''Leucaena leucocephala'' is an [[allelopathic]] tree. Phytotoxic allelochemicals, such as [[mimosine]] and certain phenolic compounds, including [[p-hydroxycinnamic acid]], [[protocatechuic acid]], and [[gallic acid]], have been identified in the leaves of the species.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1007/BF01012362 | doi=10.1007/BF01012362 | title=Allelopathic research of subtropical vegetation in Taiwan | year=1986 |author1-link=Chou Chang-hung | last1=Chou | first1=Chang -Hung | last2=Kuo | first2=Yaw -Lun | journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology | volume=12 | issue=6 | pages=1431–1448 | pmid=24307122 | bibcode=1986JCEco..12.1431C | s2cid=25942600 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> Bioherbicidal activity of ''L. leucocephala'' on terrestrial plants<ref>Hong NH, Xuan TD, Eiji T, Hiroyuki T, Mitsuhiro M, Khanh TD (2003) Screening for allelopathic potential of higher plants from Southeast Asia. Crop Protection 22:829–836</ref><ref>John J, Narwal SS (2003) Allelopathic plants. 9. Leucaena leucocephala (Lam.) de Wit. Allelopath J 12:13–36 OpenURL</ref> and aquatic weed [[water hyacinth]]<ref>Chai TT, Ooh KF, Ooi PW, Chue PS, Wong FC (2013) [http://www.as-botanicalstudies.com/content/54/1/8#B17 ''Leucaena leucocephala'' leachate compromised membrane integrity, respiration and antioxidative defence of water hyacinth leaf tissues]. Botanical Studies 54: 8.</ref> were reported.

==In culture==
The state of [[Oaxaca]] in Mexico derives its name from the [[Nahuatl]] word {{Lang|nhe|huaxyacac}}, the name for ''Leucaena leucocephala'' trees that are found around [[Oaxaca City]].<ref name="consular">{{cite web |last=Consular |first=Gaceta |date=October 1996 |title=Oaxaca |url=http://www.mexconnect.com/articles/2815-oaxaca |access-date=August 15, 2010 |publisher=MexConnect}}</ref>
